title: test-0052-SCI-PHY-EYE10
passage: The human eye functions like a camera, using a flexible crystalline lens to focus light onto the retina. To see nearby objects, the ciliary muscles contract, causing the eye lens to become thicker and more curved, which increases its converging power. Conversely, for distant objects, the muscles relax, making the lens thinner and flatter. Sometimes, the eye loses its ability to focus properly. In myopia, the eyeball becomes too long, causing light from distant objects to focus in front of the retina, meaning the person cannot see distant objects clearly. In hypermetropia, the eyeball is too short, and the eye struggles to focus on nearby objects without extra effort from the ciliary muscles. Regarding the sky, sunlight enters the atmosphere and hits tiny gas molecules. These small particles scatter shorter blue wavelengths more strongly than longer red wavelengths, which is why the sky appears blue. At sunset, light travels through a thicker layer of the atmosphere, scattering away most blue light and leaving only the longer red wavelengths to reach our eyes. This change in color is purely a result of atmospheric scattering, not because the sun itself is changing temperature or cooling down. Finally, stars appear to twinkle because their light undergoes continuous refraction through shifting layers of the atmosphere, not because their actual brightness changes.
summary: To see nearby objects, the ciliary muscles contract, making the eye lens thicker and more curved, which helps it converge more strongly. At sunset, the light travels through a thicker layer of the atmosphere, so most blue light is scattered and only the red light gets to us.
